opus-5.5.text:
I think the deepest source of uncertainty usually isn't the near-term question of "does this program work?" With a lot of interventions, especially in global health, you can get reasonably confident about the direct effects. You can run trials, look at the evidence, and say, okay, this bednet distribution probably averts a certain number of deaths from malaria. That's hard, but it's tractable.

The harder thing is what happens downstream, over the long run. Every intervention ripples out into the world in ways that are mostly invisible to us. You save a life, and that person goes on to have a family, contribute to their economy, and affect population growth, institutions, and maybe the trajectory of their country. Each of those effects has further effects. When you try to ask what the net effect on the world is over the next hundred or thousand years, you realize you have very little idea. And those long-run effects could plausibly dwarf the direct effects you measured so carefully.

So there's this uncomfortable situation where the part you can measure might be a small fraction of what actually matters, and the part that matters most is the part where you're basically guessing. It's not even clear you know the sign. Something that looks robustly good could, through some chain of consequences, turn out to be neutral or harmful. The reverse is also possible.

I don't think the right response is paralysis. In practice, I try to do a few things. One is to look for interventions where the case for being good seems robust across a lot of different ways the world could go. Another is to take seriously that if long-run effects dominate, maybe you should be thinking more directly about the long run. That's part of why I've ended up focusing so much on things like transformative AI, where it seems more plausible that we're at a pivotal point that could shape the whole future. And a third is to hold a kind of humility and diversification across worldviews, rather than betting everything on one chain of reasoning, because I know my picture of how things play out is pretty fragile.

But if you ask me where the real uncertainty lives, it's there. It's less "did this work?" and more "what did this ultimately set in motion?"

r001.rationale: The response says an intervention’s downstream effects over hundreds or thousands of years are hard to predict, may dwarf measured direct effects, and leave its overall effect’s sign uncertain.

r002.rationale: The response discusses present interventions’ future consequences, but does not state that present actions can affect past generations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the deeper source of uncertainty is that for most interventions, the thing you can measure is not the thing you actually care about. You can measure whether bednets got distributed, whether malaria cases went down in the trial villages. What you care about is whether, decades later, the world is better in some overall sense because of what you did. And the gap between those two is enormous, and most of it is not something you can study.

Part of it is just empirical: the long-run effects of anything are hard to trace. Does saving a life in a poor country increase or decrease population growth, and is that good or bad? Does economic growth in one place lead to more global stability or to more conflict? These aren't questions where I think we lack the right study. They're questions where I'm not sure a study could resolve them even in principle.

But I think the bigger piece is that we're often uncertain about what "good" even means at the scale we're trying to operate on. We can be fairly confident that a child not dying of malaria is good. We're much less confident in the whole picture of what a flourishing world looks like, or how to weigh different people's interests, or how much to care about the far future versus the present. When you try to be rigorous about doing good, you quickly bump into moral philosophy questions that smart people have been arguing about for thousands of years without consensus.

So my honest attitude is that I'm operating under a kind of double uncertainty. I don't know the full consequences of what I'm doing, and I'm not fully sure how I'd evaluate them if I did. What I try to do is find actions that look robustly good across a range of plausible views, keep a lot of humility about my ability to model the world, and be willing to update when things turn out differently than I expected. I don't think you can do better than that, and I think pretending you can is where a lot of people get into trouble.

r001.rationale: The response identifies uncertainty about long-run consequences and how to weigh the far future against the present when judging whether an intervention makes the world better overall.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that present actions can affect past generations; it discusses consequences for the future and present.

astra-6.text:
I think the deeper uncertainty is that we don’t really know how to connect the effects we can measure to everything we ultimately care about. You can have very good evidence that an intervention improves someone’s health or raises their income, and that’s a real reason to be excited about it. But that doesn’t settle what its effects will be over decades or centuries.

It changes what people do, which changes what other people do, and those consequences spread out beyond what you can study directly. At that point, you’re relying on a broader view about how the world works: whether improving lives today generally helps put the future on a better trajectory, for example.

So I wouldn’t say the uncertainty is just, ‘Did we run a good enough study?’ Some of it is uncertainty about the framework we’re using to interpret the study. And that’s much harder to resolve by collecting more data on the immediate outcome.

r001.rationale: It contrasts measurable immediate benefits with effects over decades or centuries, and says those consequences spread beyond what can be studied directly, identifying long-term and intergenerational evaluation as a source of uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It discusses effects on other people and the future, but does not say present actions can affect past generations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the deepest uncertainty is that we don’t really understand the long-run consequences of what we do. You can have pretty good evidence that an intervention improves health or raises incomes, and that’s important. But if you keep asking, “And then what happens?” you eventually get beyond what the evidence can tell you.

That doesn’t mean the intervention is bad, or that we should be paralysed. It means there’s a distinction between being confident about a measurable outcome and being confident that the world is ultimately better because of it. The latter depends on a lot of judgments about how the world works, what the future is going to look like, and what matters morally. And those judgments are much harder to check.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about long-run consequences and future outcomes, but does not identify evaluating effects across all generations.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that present actions can affect past generations.
